title: Fifty-Three Guineas
passage:
A subscriber to the book society had one volume out at a time and might keep it a fortnight. The second fortnight needed no asking. The mark ‘cont.’ was written against the entry, and nothing was charged before the twenty-ninth day, when a penny a day began. What stopped the second fortnight was the slate by the door, where a subscriber set down the title he wanted; a volume so claimed came in on the fourteenth day. The slate was rubbed clean every week and no copy of it was kept. The shelves stood over a saddler’s shop in a market town twenty miles from navigable water, and the ledger ran from 1827 to 1835, every loan entered with its dates out and in, the volume and the name. Fifty-three subscribers paid a guinea a year, and three of them chose what was bought. A book of travels went out 41 times in those nine years; 39 of the loans came in on the fourteenth day, and two were continued. A volume of sermons went out nine times and was continued seven times. Ralph Jarrett, a currier, had more loans against his name than anybody else. Eleven of the fifty-three paid their guinea in each of the nine years and carried nothing home. A volume might be fetched by a servant or a child of the house, and the ledger named neither.
– Yvonne Hobbermarsh

options.text: Subscribers gave up the travels at the fortnight with another reader waiting for it.

questions.rationale: Option A is the answer, and the passage sets down the two facts that make it without ever joining them. The first is the society’s own rule. A second fortnight cost nothing and needed no application, so a borrower who wanted longer simply kept the book, and the one thing that brought a volume in on the fourteenth day was the slate, where another subscriber had set down the title. The second fact is the count: of 41 loans of the travels, 39 came in on the fourteenth day and two ran on. Thirty-nine loans over nine years gave up a free fortnight apiece, and under that rule the natural reading is that the title stood claimed while it was out. A claims that and no more. It does not say the travels were the best-read book in the town, it does not say the borrowers had finished with them, and it does not name the readers who were waiting, because the slate that would have named them was rubbed clean each week and never copied. B is the fine misreading, and it lives off the passage’s own words, since a penny a day is there and so is the fortnight; but the charge began on the twenty-ninth day, and the sermons were continued in seven of their nine loans without anything falling due. C is the outside-knowledge trap and the most respectable of the three, because book societies of the period did commonly favour a general meeting that voted the year’s purchases; this one did not work that way, and the passage says in one clause that three of the fifty-three chose what was bought. D takes the sentence about the eleven who carried nothing home and attaches the obvious story to it, that a name with no loans against it belongs to a member who had drifted out of the society; the same sentence refutes it, since those eleven paid their guinea in each of the nine years. Each of B, C and D is refuted by a clause in the passage that a careful reader can point to.

generator_meta.period_detail_note: Audited item by item against ordinary English book-society and subscription-library practice of the 1820s and 1830s. A guinea a year for a small-town society is in the normal range, and the guinea survived as a money of account long after the coin stopped being struck in 1816. One volume out at a time is the standard entitlement of a single share. A fortnight is a standard loan term for such a society. An overdue charge of a penny a day is at the low end of the usual penny-to-twopence range. Purchases chosen by a small committee of members, rather than by the whole subscription, is one of the two normal arrangements - the other, a general meeting that votes the year's books, is what distractor C offers and what this society is said not to do. A want list kept on a slate and rubbed out is an ordinary piece of counter equipment and an ordinary reason for such a list not to survive. Shelves in a hired room over a shop is the usual housing. WHAT A LEDGER WOULD AND WOULD NOT RECORD is the load-bearing period point and is handled explicitly: a borrowing register of this kind records the date out, the date in, a short title and the subscriber's name, and it does not record why a loan ended, who in the household read the book, or what stood on the want list - the passage says the last of these in terms and the closing sentence says the second. NO BOOK TITLES ARE PRINTED. The two books are named by kind ('a book of travels', 'a volume of sermons'), which is how a historian writes when the register's own titles are two or three words long; this borrows no real title and invents none, and so removes a law-16 surface rather than adding one. Both kinds are the right kinds: travels and sermons are the two commonest categories in surviving book-society catalogues of the period.

reasoning: The instruction for this item was explicitly conservative: fix only if a minimal rewording removes the ambiguity without changing the proposition, the option’s length band or its variable, and otherwise leave it and record. No candidate met all three.

The ambiguity is real but narrow and it cannot be removed by a one-word swap. ‘the travels’ is plural in form and singular in reference (the passage’s ‘A book of travels’), so ‘it’ agrees with the referent and ‘the fortnight’ agrees with the surface - which is precisely why the pronoun can be misread. Replacing it needs a full noun phrase, and every full noun phrase costs a word.

Variants measured with mech.tokenize and rejected. (a) G-ENG’s own ‘for the book’: 14 -> 15 tokens, which makes the key JOINT-LONGEST with distractor B at 15 and spends the ‘key not the longest’ property that this option set currently holds outright; B is also the ‘fine misreading’ a test-wise student is already drawn to, so a longest-tie between exactly those two is the worst place to spend it. (b) dropping the pronoun (‘… with another reader waiting.’): 13 tokens, which makes the key tie D as the SHORTEST and leaves the object of ‘waiting’ unstated. (d) reordering to put ‘it’ next to ‘the travels’ holds 14 tokens but strands ‘at the fortnight’ at the end, where it attaches to ‘waiting’ - a new ambiguity for an old one.

Only one of three G-ENG votes stopped on it, the verdict is a flag and not lethal, G-STEM r2 passed q:1 and recorded ‘Option lengths are evenly matched at 14 to 15 words each, so there is no length cue’, G-DISTRACTOR r2 passed with zero findings, and G-KEY solved q1 on both blind legs with the pronoun in place.
